planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chequers keeps more green in its foliage than the solid-silver cultivars, showing a single silvery stripe down each leaf, and bears rosy-purple flowers in late spring.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting it away from hot afternoon sun and heavy summer humidity, which it tolerates less readily than more refined modern selections. Chequers keeps a higher proportion of green in its heart-shaped leaves than the solid-silver lamium cultivars, marked instead by a single narrow silvery stripe running down the center of each leaf, and produces whorls of small, hooded, rosy-purple flowers from late spring on into fall. It roots along its trailing stems as it spreads, gradually forming a dense, semi-evergreen mat that suppresses weeds beneath trees and shrubs, and it holds up reasonably well in drier shade once established. Divide congested clumps in spring if the patch outgrows its space or starts to thin in the center.

common_name: Red Nancy Lamium (Silver-Leaf Magenta-Flowered Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Red Nancy is essentially a magenta-flowered sport of White Nancy, sharing the same silvery foliage but trading the white blooms for rich pink-purple ones.

directions: Plant in average, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, avoiding soggy sites in winter. Red Nancy shares its silvery, narrowly green-edged foliage with the classic White Nancy but swaps the white flowers for whorls of rich magenta-pink blooms carried on red-tinged stems from late spring into fall, giving a warmer accent among the pale foliage. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover mat that fills in quickly beneath trees and shrubs. Shear the mat back if it looks ragged after flowering to promote fresh foliage, and divide crowded clumps in spring to control spread or generate new plants.

common_name: Pink Chablis Lamium (Silvery-White Cotton-Candy-Pink Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Pink Chablis is a newer patented selection with nearly solid silvery-white leaves and clear pink flowers over a long summer bloom period.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist, in partial shade to full shade, keeping it out of hot midday sun that can scorch the pale leaves. Pink Chablis carries oval, toothed leaves with a strong silver sheen edged narrowly in dark green, and produces spikes of hooded, cotton-candy pink flowers over an unusually long stretch from early to late summer, outlasting the spring-only bloom window of many older lamium cultivars. Its low, mounding, trailing habit spreads gradually to knit together a tidy groundcover mat that pairs well with variegated hostas and ferns in a shaded border. Trim lightly after the first flush of bloom to tidy the mat and encourage rebloom later in the season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Aureum stands apart from the silver-leaved lamium cultivars with gold to chartreuse foliage marked by a pale central stripe, topped with pink flowers.

directions: Plant in average, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to heavy shade, keeping it out of direct sun, which quickly scorches the gold foliage. Aureum breaks from the usual silver-and-green lamium palette with heart-shaped leaves in bright gold to chartreuse, faintly marked with silvery streaks down the center, an effect that glows in dim woodland light more than any silver cultivar can. Clusters of soft pink, hooded flowers appear in late spring above the colored foliage, drawing bees to an otherwise shaded corner of the garden. It roots readily wherever its trailing stems touch soil, making it simple to divide for spreading along a shaded bank or rock wall, and established plants tolerate drier shade than the color might suggest.
